title: Your standards are too low.
summary: After backlash over his 6/10 grade on a French natural bodybuilder's physique, NH argues that high standards and a strong, criticism-proof ego drive progress. He says natural limits are mostly cultural, uses the Pygmalion effect and a Pascal's-wager argument to show high standards always pay, and attacks genetics excuses, blackpill lifters and comforting mediocrity.
claims: Setting standards too low leads to both a weak character and a mediocre physique
He graded a top French natural bodybuilder (Ovak, per captions) 6/10 on a community post and was accused of unrealistic standards and blackpilling
French expert Michael Gundill, who coaches IFBB pros, was teaching in the 1990s what science-based influencers now copy; he grades harshly because he is used to the top of the sport
Gundill told that natural lifter he had small legs, lacked abs and chest and had bad calves; the lifter looked hurt, then turned the criticism into motivation, a lesson in standards
The most important acquired trait, beyond genetic potential, is responding to criticism by raising your standards instead of resisting it
To accept that a better version of you exists you must accept your current version is incomplete, which many people cannot do
An ego only needs protecting if it is weak; a solid ego takes blows and stays intact
A big ego is not bad and ego death in bodybuilding is the death of progression; the problem is an ego that grows big but fragile and rejects criticism
Advanced lifters and influencers who keep the same body for 5-7 years have not hit a natural limit; they stopped striving because they think they know everything
See your body as a vessel for the self, a project permanently under construction that can always improve
The natural limit is a cultural limit, not a biological one
The average gym lifter is about 170 lb in France and about 180 lb in the USA, a gap explained by culture, not biology
France has an anti-bodybuilding culture with no muscular icons, so standards are so low that he, Ovak or GVS would be accused of steroids there
US fitness culture (gyms everywhere, movies, the American dream, the Protestant work ethic) raises standards and results
Pygmalion effect: people told they will do well do better; surround yourself with bigger natural lifters and with thoughts of greatness
Records that stood for 10-30 years get broken repeatedly once one person breaks them, showing belief was the limit
People do not attempt goals mostly from fear of how failure would feel; saying it is impossible really means I am not enough
High standards are not entitlement: someone else's physique shows how high the ceiling is, not that you will get it
If seeing better physiques fills you with resentment, the problem is yours, not the person showing the standard
The mediocre want everyone mediocre; people who complain about fake natties often care less about the lying than about unrealistic expectations making them feel worse
Expectations do not need to be realistic; standards tied to what you know you can accomplish are by definition low
Starting out he would have laughed at the idea of reaching 220 lb with 18-inch arms and 28-inch legs; he just kept training to see where he would go
Be delusional: refuse to set your own limits and train expecting to keep growing; limits exist but you cannot locate them and self-assessments almost always underestimate
Believing in low potential becomes a self-fulfilling excuse: low standards bring low results, which then justify the excuse
He rates his own genetics 5/10, roughly average, so he must work twice as hard as an 8 or 9
Blaming genetics is cowardice: it moves responsibility outside yourself and admits you think your essence is worthless
If you are never disappointed you are not aiming high enough; always succeeding means you take too few risks
A Pascal's-wager argument for potential: with high standards even failure leaves you with something great, while low standards give little even when you succeed
A good physique would have no value if it were easy; the point is that it is possible
As an influencer he would rather frustrate people with high standards than tell them their 14-inch arms and four-pack are fine
The average male cannot do one pull-up or deadlift his bodyweight, has small arms and is active under 45 minutes a week; every able-bodied man should manage these basics
Fitness exists to breed above-average people; an elite core shows society what is possible and raises everyone's standards, an aristocracy of body and mind open to anyone who works
Positive reinforcement has its place and any activity beats none, but people stick with fitness more when they believe they can achieve great things
exercises: the average male cannot do one; every able-bodied man should
every able-bodied man should deadlift his bodyweight
